summary:
NIRAN — The Memory of Fires is a web application that harmonizes MODIS and VIIRS active fire hotspot records from NASA FIRMS into a unified, interactive Burning Activity Calendar. Built for Challenge #8 of the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, NIRAN addresses a real scientific gap: two decades of NASA satellite fire data exist, but they are split across two sensors with different spatial resolutions (MODIS at 1 km, VIIRS at 375 m) that cannot be directly compared, leaving emergency managers without a consistent picture of fire activity over time.

NIRAN solves this by computing region-specific calibration ratios on the period where both sensors overlap, producing one continuous time series from 2020 to 2025. Users can spin a 3D interactive globe, pick any country (Morocco, Australia, Brazil and counting), and instantly see the burning activity calendar — a year-by-month heatmap that reveals seasonal patterns and flags anomalies at a glance. The tool also shows near-real-time detections (20,515 live hotspots in the last 7 days) and lets users download the harmonized dataset as CSV.

NIRAN matters because fire seasons are growing longer and more intense under climate change. Emergency managers, scientists, and land managers need one trusted, harmonized record to anticipate critical periods, validate climate models, and plan controlled burns. NIRAN turns fragmented raw satellite data into one shared memory of fires — actionable, visual, and global.
details:
What it does and how it works

NIRAN is a live web application accessible at https://niran-the-memory-of-fires.onrender.com. It takes raw NASA FIRMS hotspot records from both MODIS (Terra, Aqua; 1 km resolution; active since 2000) and VIIRS (Suomi-NPP, NOAA-20; 375 m resolution; active since 2012), harmonizes them into a single consistent time series, and exposes them through three integrated views:

  1. Interactive 3D globe — Users drag to spin the Earth and click any country to focus the analysis on that region. Currently Morocco, Australia, and Brazil are pre-loaded; the architecture supports any country.
  2. Burning Activity Calendar — A year-by-month heatmap (Jan–Dec × 2020–2025) with a color ramp where each cell shows the number of detected hotspots. Green = low activity, orange = medium, red = critical. Seasonal patterns and anomalies become instantly visible.
  3. Near-real-time layer — A live counter of detections from the last 7 days, currently at 20,515 hotspots, with above/below/within-normal indicators comparing current activity against the historical baseline.

The harmonization method

On the 2020–2024 period where both MODIS and VIIRS are operating, NIRAN computes the average VIIRS-to-MODIS detection ratio per region. Because VIIRS detects 2–3× more fires than MODIS for the same event (due to its finer spatial resolution), this ratio is applied as a calibration factor to make the two sensors tell one consistent story. After harmonization, the sensor of origin no longer matters — patterns, trends, and anomalies become the focus.

Benefits and expected impact

NIRAN serves three concrete audiences:

  • Emergency managers can spot anomalies like the Mediterranean August 2023 spike and pre-position resources before the peak of the season.
  • Scientists get a harmonized dataset they can use to validate climate models and study long-term fire trends without sensor artifacts.
  • Land managers can plan controlled burns at the right time and monitor sensitive ecosystems.

The tool is live, multi-region, and scalable — adding a new country is a configuration change, not a code change.

Tools, languages, and software used

  • Data source: NASA FIRMS API (official MODIS and VIIRS active fire products)
  • Backend / data processing: Python (Pandas, NumPy) for harmonization and aggregation
  • Frontend / visualization: Streamlit-style dashboard with a 3D interactive globe component
  • Deployment: Render (live at https://niran-the-memory-of-fires.onrender.com)
  • Version control: GitHub (public repo, linked in the project page)
  • AI tools: Used for code scaffolding and documentation; reviewed and integrated by the team.

What is creative about it

  1. First harmonized public web app for MODIS/VIIRS — Most wildfire dashboards display raw hotspots; NIRAN solves the underlying scientific incompatibility.
  2. The Memory of Fires concept — Every fire leaves a trace; NIRAN captures that memory across years. The name and the storytelling make the project memorable, not just functional.
  3. 3D interactive globe — Users spin the Earth instead of panning a flat map, which makes the global nature of fire activity tangible.
  4. Multi-country comparison — Morocco, Australia, and Brazil in the same tool, allowing cross-region pattern discovery.

Considerations the team took into account

  • Scientific validity of the harmonization — Choosing a region-specific ratio calibration rather than a naive concatenation, to avoid the artificial 2012 jump that breaks the time series.
  • Performance and usability — Live rendering of 20,000+ detections without lag, in any browser, no login required.
  • Real users first — The UX is designed for emergency managers, scientists, and land managers, not for the general public.
  • Scalability — The architecture supports extending the harmonized archive back to 2000 and adding new regions without redesigning the app.
  • NASA data at the core — Every number shown comes from NASA FIRMS. No third-party fire APIs were used, in compliance with the challenge brief.
